--- title: "The coastal survey" description: "The simulated survey the course works on: what a station records, the names for the parts of a data table, which columns move together, why its stations are fewer independent observations than rows, and the four files built from it." order: 1 categories: [marine-data, eda] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Most examples come from this survey Almost every example in this course comes from one dataset, a survey of the seabed along a stretch of coast. Once you know it well, later pages can spend your attention on the method instead of the data. This page shows what one row of the survey holds, names the parts of a data table, shows which columns move together, and counts how many independent observations the table really contains. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## A station is one visit At each **station** a ship stops, measures the water from the surface to the seabed, records what the seabed is made of, and takes a sample of the seabed to count one species of animal. One station is one row of the table. ::: {.diagram} ![What the survey records at one station. The ship's position and the date say where and when; an instrument lowered through the water measures it; the seabed is described; and a sample from the seabed gives the count of the species.](img/survey-station.svg){fig-alt="On the left, a ship at the sea surface lowers an instrument through the water and a sampler to the seabed, with an arrow down the side marking depth. On the right, four cards: where and when (longitude, latitude, survey year, season); the water (depth, temperature, salinity, chlorophyll); the species (abundance, the animals counted, and present, yes or no); and the seabed (substrate: sand, mud, gravel or rock). Dashed lines join the ship, the instrument, the sampler and the seabed to their cards."} ::: ## Twelve columns describe each station The survey has 800 stations, visited between 2018 and 2023, in all four seasons. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() glimpse(survey) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Rows: 800 #> Columns: 12 #> $ station_id "ST0001", "ST0002", "ST0003", "ST0004", "ST0005", "S… #> $ survey_year 2021, 2020, 2023, 2022, 2021, 2020, 2021, 2023, 2021… #> $ season summer, winter, summer, autumn, spring, summer, summ… #> $ longitude 141.7377, 141.6164, 140.5556, 140.5318, 141.9513, 14… #> $ latitude 42.3526, 41.7999, 41.7484, 41.7782, 42.4716, 41.0464… #> $ depth_m 99.2, 134.7, 52.3, 90.8, 125.0, 60.1, 16.6, 58.8, 53… #> $ temperature_c 11.15, 4.42, 14.69, 10.02, 6.35, 14.08, 14.86, 10.30… #> $ salinity_psu 33.26, 34.20, 33.67, 33.47, 34.22, 33.91, 33.04, 33.… #> $ chlorophyll_mg_m3 2.061, 0.446, 1.642, 1.822, 1.641, 1.153, 1.296, 6.1… #> $ substrate gravel, mud, mud, mud, sand, gravel, gravel, sand, m… #> $ abundance 15, 0, 0, 21, 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 3, 8, 9, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4,… #> $ present yes, no, no, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes,… ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey survey = load_coastal_survey() survey.info() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> RangeIndex: 800 entries, 0 to 799 #> Data columns (total 12 columns): #> # Column Non-Null Count Dtype #> --- ------ -------------- ----- #> 0 station_id 800 non-null str #> 1 survey_year 800 non-null int64 #> 2 season 800 non-null category #> 3 longitude 800 non-null float64 #> 4 latitude 800 non-null float64 #> 5 depth_m 800 non-null float64 #> 6 temperature_c 800 non-null float64 #> 7 salinity_psu 800 non-null float64 #> 8 chlorophyll_mg_m3 800 non-null float64 #> 9 substrate 800 non-null category #> 10 abundance 800 non-null int64 #> 11 present 800 non-null category #> dtypes: category(3), float64(6), int64(2), str(1) #> memory usage: 59.2 KB ``` ::: ::: ::: | Column | What it is | Values in the survey | | --- | --- | --- | | `station_id` | A label for the station | ST0001, ST0002, … | | `survey_year` | The year of the visit | 2018 to 2023 | | `season` | The season of the visit | spring, summer, autumn, winter | | `longitude`, `latitude` | Where the station is, in degrees | a box about 206 by 222 km | | `depth_m` | Depth of the seabed, in metres | 5 to 195 | | `temperature_c` | Water temperature, in °C | 1.9 to 16.0 | | `salinity_psu` | How salty the water is, in practical salinity units (PSU), close to grams of salt per kilogram of seawater | 32.6 to 34.8 | | `chlorophyll_mg_m3` | Chlorophyll, in mg per m³: a measure of how much phytoplankton the water holds | 0.1 to 13.8 | | `substrate` | What the seabed is made of | sand, mud, gravel, rock | | `abundance` | The number of animals of the species counted in the sample | 0 to 40 | | `present` | Whether the species was found at all | yes at 78% of stations | Most columns are numbers; `season`, `substrate` and `present` are categories, which a model has to handle differently (see [Kinds of marine data](marine-data-types.qmd)). ## Each row is an observation A data table holds one **observation** in each row: one thing that was measured, here one station. Most pages use one of the two species columns, `abundance` or `present`, as the **outcome** a model predicts, and some of the other columns as its **inputs**. [Types of learning](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd) introduced both terms. Machine learning grew up in computer science and in statistics separately, so each part of the table has several names, and the literature uses all of them: | In this course | Also called | What it is | | --- | --- | --- | | **Observation** | row, instance, example, sample, case | One thing that was measured | | **Input** | feature, predictor, covariate, independent variable, attribute | Something known about it | | **Outcome** | response, target, dependent variable, $y$ | What the model predicts | | **Label** | class, annotation, ground truth | A known outcome, often one a person assigned | Beware of "sample": in machine learning it means one observation, in field science the whole collection. What one row should be is a scientific choice. A survey that returns to the same sites could have one row per sample, per visit, or per site, and the right one follows from the question: a question about a site's character needs one row per site, not one per visit. ## The shelf deepens offshore ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(survey, aes(longitude, latitude, colour = depth_m)) + geom_point(size = 1.6) + scale_colour_viridis_c(direction = -1, name = "Depth (m)") + coord_quickmap() + labs(x = "Longitude (°E)", y = "Latitude (°N)", title = "Stations coloured by depth") + theme(legend.position = "right") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where the stations are. Depth rises steadily from west to east, so the survey runs from the coast out across the shelf.](the-coastal-survey_files/figure-html/fig-map-1.png){#fig-map fig-alt='A map of 800 points in a rectangle of longitude 140 to 142.5 and latitude 41 to 43. The points are coloured by depth: pale yellow in the west, at about 10 to 40 metres, shading through green to dark purple in the east, at 150 to 195 metres.' width=1400} ::: ::: The stations are spread evenly over the area rather than laid on a grid. Stations close together share more than their depth: they sit in the same patch of sea, so their counts tend to be alike. That matters when stations are held back to test a model, as the count of sites further down shows. ## Depth shapes the water The water measurements do not vary independently. Deeper water here is colder and saltier: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_temp <- ggplot(survey, aes(depth_m, temperature_c)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.35, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Temperature (°C)", title = "Colder with depth") p_sal <- ggplot(survey, aes(depth_m, salinity_psu)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.35, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + labs(x = "Depth (m)", y = "Salinity (PSU)", title = "Saltier with depth") p_temp + p_sal ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Temperature and salinity against depth. Both change with depth, so a model given all three is given partly the same information three times.](the-coastal-survey_files/figure-html/fig-depth-1.png){#fig-depth fig-alt='Two scatter plots against depth from 0 to 200 metres. Left: temperature falls from mostly 8 to 16 °C in shallow water to 2 to 8 °C near 200 metres, with wide scatter. Right: salinity rises from about 33 PSU in shallow water to about 34.5 in deep water, in a tighter band.' width=1700} ::: ::: A **correlation** puts a number on this, from −1 (one always falls as the other rises) through 0 (no straight-line link) to 1 (they always rise together). Depth and salinity have a correlation of 0.72; depth and temperature −0.47. Columns that move together like this are normal in marine data, and they are behind the warning in [Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd): a column can help a model predict simply because it travels with another one. ## Most stations hold only a few animals ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(survey, aes(abundance)) + geom_bar(fill = ml_palette[["green"]]) + labs(x = "Animals counted at the station", y = "Stations", title = "Many small counts, a few large ones") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The count of the species at each station. Most counts are small, zero is common, and a few stations hold many more animals than the rest.](the-coastal-survey_files/figure-html/fig-abundance-1.png){#fig-abundance fig-alt='A bar chart of abundance from 0 to 40. The tallest bar is at 0, with about 180 stations, then 1 with about 140 and 2 with about 95; the bars shrink steadily after that, and only a handful of stations have more than 20 animals.' width=1400} ::: ::: The species was absent at 22% of stations, half the stations hold 2 animals or fewer, and the largest count is 40. Counts shaped like this, piled up near zero with a long tail, are typical of survey catches, and they are why the course treats abundance with some care. ## The stations come from far fewer sites The survey returns to fixed sites, and each visit to a site is one station. The clean file leaves the site out, but the raw file, the survey as it came off the ship, keeps it in a column `site_id`: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw <- load_coastal_survey_raw() tibble( rows = nrow(raw), `unique rows` = nrow(distinct(raw)), `distinct sites` = n_distinct(raw$site_id) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| rows| unique rows| distinct sites| |----:|-----------:|--------------:| | 815| 800| 160|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_raw raw = load_coastal_survey_raw() pd.DataFrame({ "rows": [len(raw)], "unique rows": [len(raw.drop_duplicates())], "distinct sites": [raw["site_id"].nunique()], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | rows | unique rows | distinct sites | |-------:|--------------:|-----------------:| | 815 | 800 | 160 | ::: ::: ::: A model treats every row as independent evidence. These rows are not, in three ways: - **Duplicates.** 15 rows are the same station entered twice. They add nothing but count double, and a copy in the test data is predicted perfectly without the model having learned anything; see [Avoiding information leakage](information-leakage.qmd). - **Repeat visits.** The 800 unique rows come from only 160 sites, about 5 visits each. Visits to one site share the water and the seabed, so they are closer to repeats of one observation than to separate ones. Treating them as separate is called **pseudo-replication**. - **Nearby sites.** Two sites a few kilometres apart share a water mass and a depth; [Spatial and temporal dependence](../06-assumptions-limitations/spatial-and-temporal-dependence.qmd) comes back to this. So the number of independent observations is nearer 160 than 800, and a score computed as if it were 800 looks better than it should. The fix is not to throw rows away, since repeat visits show how much a site varies, but to keep each site's rows together when the data are split to test a model. [Splitting the data](splitting-data.qmd) shows how. ## One survey in four files The clean survey is the one on this page. Three more files are made from it, each for a particular job: ::: {.diagram} ![The clean survey and the three files made from it. The raw file is the same station visits before anyone tidied them; the truth file holds the average count the simulation expected at each station; the community file counts 24 species at the same stations.](img/survey-files.svg){fig-alt="A card on the left for the clean survey, 800 stations and 12 columns, used on almost every page. Arrows labelled made from it lead to three cards on the right: raw, the same visits as they came off the ship, with errors to find and fix, used in this section; truth, the average count expected at each station, which no real survey has, used to check models; and community, counts of 24 species at the same stations, used for finding groups."} ::: Each has its own loader, so a page never reads a file directly: - `load_coastal_survey()`: the clean survey. - `load_coastal_survey_raw()`: the same visits with the errors of a real field file, such as impossible depths and misspelt categories. The rest of this section finds and fixes them, starting with [Exploring and cleaning the data](exploring-and-cleaning.qmd). - `load_coastal_survey_truth()`: the average count the simulation expected at each station, before chance added its noise. - `load_coastal_community()`: counts of 24 species at the same stations, for finding groups of stations. ## The true answers are known The survey is simulated: a script decided how the species responds to its surroundings, then drew counts that follow those rules with realistic noise added. So unlike a real survey, this one has known answers. Later pages fit a model, read what it found, and only then check it against the rules the simulation used. This page leaves those rules out on purpose. The skill the course teaches is reading a model without knowing the answer in advance, which is the only way a real survey is ever read. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - One station is one visit and one row: where and when, the water, the seabed, and the count of one species. - Each row is an **observation**; most pages predict `abundance` or `present`, the outcome, from some of the other columns, the inputs. - Depth, temperature and salinity move together, so they partly carry the same information. - The 800 stations come from 160 sites, so the table holds far fewer independent observations than rows. Keep each site's rows together when splitting. - The clean survey has three companion files: raw, truth and community, each with its own loader. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Plot `abundance` against `depth_m`, then against `temperature_c`. Does the species seem to prefer a particular depth, or a particular temperature? Write your guess down; later pages will let you check it. 2. For your own data, write one sentence saying what one observation is, and one naming what makes two of your rows share information.
